title: Multi-Digit Multiplication in Grade 4: Area Model to Column Method + Free Quiz
meta_title: Multi Digit Multiplication Grade 4 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach multi digit multiplication in Grade 4: area model and partial products first, then the column method plus the place-holder zero. Free quiz inside.
excerpt: A Grade 4 child who can do 7 × 8 still freezes at 34 × 27. The fix is not more speed — it is meaning first. Here is the order that works, from the box model to the compact column method, with a free quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 4 child 34 × 27 and watch what happens. If tables are solid, they can rattle off 7 × 8 without blinking — but a two-digit by two-digit sum makes many of them stall, or worse, line up the digits and add. That gap is the whole story of Grade 4 maths. Multi digit multiplication in Grade 4 is not a new fact to memorise; it is a procedure built on tables the child already knows, and the trick is to teach the meaning before the shortcut. Rush straight to the column method and you get children who multiply the ones, forget the tens, and never notice the answer is impossibly small.

I am assuming your child knows tables 1 to 10 fluently. If they do not, stop here and fix that first — every method below leans on instant recall of single-digit products. What follows is the order I use: build the picture with the area model and partial products, then compress it into the standard column algorithm, then teach estimation so the child can catch their own mistakes.

Start with the area (box) model, not the algorithm

The area model draws multiplication as a rectangle split into parts. To do 34 × 27, break each number by place value: 34 becomes 30 and 4, and 27 becomes 20 and 7. That gives a two-by-two grid, and you fill each cell with a product the child can already do.

×304
2060080
721028

Add the four cells: 600 + 210 + 80 + 28 = 918. Notice there is no carrying to juggle in your head — every hard part is a table fact times a ten. This is why I start here. A child who has drawn the box a dozen times understands that 34 × 27 means ‘thirty-fours, twenty-seven times,’ and that the answer has to be somewhere near 30 × 30, which is 900. The box makes the size of the answer obvious.

Partial products: the bridge to the column method

Partial products are the area model written as a list instead of a grid. Same four multiplications, stacked vertically:

  • 4 × 7 = 28 (ones × ones)
  • 30 × 7 = 210 (tens × ones)
  • 4 × 20 = 80 (ones × tens)
  • 30 × 20 = 600 (tens × tens)
  • Total: 28 + 210 + 80 + 600 = 918

This is the single most useful step and the one most parents skip. Partial products keep the place value visible — the child writes 210, not a lonely 21 with a carry floating above it. Spend a week here. When your child can do 3-digit × 1-digit this way (say 243 × 6 as 1200 + 240 + 18), the compact algorithm stops being magic and becomes a shorthand they actually get.

The standard column method

Now compress. For 3-digit × 1-digit, the column method carries instead of writing full partial products. Take 243 × 6: multiply 6 × 3 = 18, write 8, carry the 1; then 6 × 4 = 24, plus the carried 1 is 25, write 5, carry 2; then 6 × 2 = 12, plus 2 is 14. Answer: 1458.

The place-holder zero — where marks are won and lost

For 2-digit × 2-digit, the column method has two lines, and the second line is where most Grade 4 errors live. Doing 34 × 27:

  • First multiply by the 7 (the ones): 7 × 34 = 238.
  • Then multiply by the 2 (which is really 20): write a 0 in the ones place of the second line first, then do 2 × 34 = 68, giving 680.
  • Add the lines: 238 + 680 = 918.

That place-holder zero is not decoration. It is there because you are multiplying by twenty, not two, so the answer must sit one place to the left. In my experience teaching ten-year-olds, the children who understand the zero are the ones who did partial products first — they know the second line is 680, so a bare 68 looks wrong to them. Teach the zero as a meaning, never as ‘a rule Miss told us.’

Estimate first, then check

Here is the counter-intuitive bit: teach estimating before the exact answer, not after. Round 34 to 30 and 27 to 30, so 34 × 27 is roughly 30 × 30 = 900. Now the child knows the answer should be near 900. If their column working spits out 91 or 4560, they can see instantly that something broke. Estimation is not a bonus skill in Grade 4; it is the child’s own error-checker.

34 × 2730 × 30 = 900918
243 × 6240 × 6 = 14401458
58 × 4360 × 40 = 24002494

A realistic practice routine

Fifteen minutes a day, four days a week. Two days on partial products so place value stays front of mind, one day on the compact column method, and one day where every problem starts with an estimate before the child is allowed to compute. That estimate-first day is the one that builds real number sense. One honest caveat: do not push for speed in Grade 4. A child who lays out 34 × 27 neatly in a minute with the zero in the right place is streets ahead of one who does it in twenty seconds and drops a digit half the time. Neatness and place value now; speed follows on its own.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a free eight-question quiz on exactly these ideas — the area model, partial products, the place-holder zero, and estimating to check. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Multi-Digit Multiplication Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the area model, partial products, the column method and estimating. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: In the area model for 34 × 27, what number goes in the cell for 30 × 20?
questions.explanation: 30 × 20 = 600. Multiply 3 × 2 = 6, then attach the two zeros.

questions.q: When you multiply 34 by the 2 in 27, why do you write a 0 first on the second line?
questions.explanation: The 2 sits in the tens place, so it means 20. The place-holder 0 shifts the answer one place left.

questions.q: Which is the best estimate for 58 × 43?
questions.explanation: Round to 60 × 40 = 2400. The exact answer, 2494, is close to this.

questions.q: Written as partial products, 43 × 5 is which of these?
A child computes 26 × 31 and gets 806. Their estimate was 30 × 30 = 900. What should they think?
questions.explanation: 806 is close to the estimate of 900, so it is reasonable. In fact 26 × 31 = 806 exactly.
5 × 7 = 35, then attach the zero from the 50, giving 350.

faq.q: Should I teach the area model or go straight to the column method?
faq.a: Start with the area model and partial products. They keep place value visible, so the child understands why 34 × 27 is near 900. The column method is a shortcut that only makes sense once the meaning is in place.

faq.q: Why does my child keep forgetting the place-holder zero?
faq.a: Almost always because they learned the column method before partial products. When a child knows the second line is really 680 (not 68), the missing zero looks obviously wrong to them. Go back to partial products for a week.

faq.q: Do tables really need to be automatic before this?
faq.a: Yes. Every step here is a table fact times a ten. If recall of 7 × 8 is slow, the child runs out of working memory before finishing the problem. Fix tables 1–10 first, then start multi-digit work.

faq.q: How do I get my child to check their own answers?
faq.a: Make them estimate before they compute. Rounding 34 × 27 to 30 × 30 = 900 gives a target; if their exact answer is far from it, they know to look again. Estimation is the built-in error-checker.
